examples.observed: Two arrows show cytosine becoming uracil and 5-methylcytosine remaining 5-methylcytosine under the bisulfite-conversion heading.
examples.safe_to_encode: Substrate base identity, depicted conversion/retention and treatment label; link these assertions to the affected DNA base feature when a method row establishes that context.
examples.not_established: A complete reaction equation, rate, reaction conditions, behavior of every other modification, or direct method ancestry.

examples.observed: Separate R-linked drawings identify cytosine, 5-methylcytosine, 5-hydroxymethylcytosine, 5-formylcytosine and 5-carboxylcytosine; altered substituents are highlighted.
examples.safe_to_encode: Named base modifications as properties of a particular molecule or preparation, retaining the R-placeholder and source image.
examples.not_established: No arrows connect these reference drawings. Do not infer a cytosine oxidation pathway or a chain of assay ancestry from their vertical order.

examples.role: explicit transformation plus matching named workflow row
examples.observed: Sidebar labels an AzNTP structure and copper-catalysed cycloaddition of 3-prime-azido-blocked cDNA to a 5-prime-hexynyl DNA adaptor; the arrow is marked Cu(I) and Rt. The ClickSeq row independently depicts RNA, semi-random primers plus AzNTP/dNTP mixture, purified single-stranded cDNA, click-ligation of an alkyne-modified adaptor, and PCR.
examples.safe_to_encode: The specific terminal handles, cDNA-to-adaptor covalent joining, named catalyst and workflow position. The complementary handles make a much more useful comparison than the word ligation alone.
examples.not_established: Exact oligo sequence, reagent ratio, yield, universal compatibility with other 3-prime blocks, or precedence over another method. Do not expand Rt into a numeric temperature.

examples.example: Acylation followed by DIBO-biotin click labeling
examples.role: two-operation chemical sequence with a source inconsistency
examples.observed: RNA poster shows RNA plus an azide-containing acylating reagent, acylation, then DIBO-biotin click attachment; caption names preparation for biotin-streptavidin purification. DNA poster counterpart labels drawn substrate/products DNA but retains a caption saying RNA.
examples.safe_to_encode: The RNA panel supports an acylation-to-click-labeling sequence and intended affinity-purification role. Preserve the DNA-panel label/caption disagreement as a source-specific conflict.
examples.not_established: Do not silently relabel the DNA panel, infer a DNA/RNA-equivalent reaction, name an attachment nucleotide position, or assign either sidebar to a method merely because it is nearby.

examples.role: reagent/entity references and a labeled class of photoactivatable nucleosides
examples.observed: DNA names pyridostatin. RNA names biotin, psoralen, 4-thiouridine, iodouridine, a bromouridine drawing, thioguanosine, 1,6-hexanediol, Br-UTP and DRB. There are no reaction arrows between these standalone entries.
examples.safe_to_encode: Source names and depicted functional groups for retrieval, with paper-specific role assigned only from a workflow or text. Keep nucleoside and nucleotide-triphosphate forms distinct.
examples.not_established: Not a common protocol or interchangeable ingredient set. The literal labels include 4-bromo uridine (5BrU) and 5-prime-Bromo-uridine (BrdU); verify naming/structure consistency before canonical chemical registration. A QR-code-decorated molecule is navigation artwork, not an assay reagent.

examples.example: G4-seq supplies the role missing from a reagent legend
examples.role: named reagent connected to a workflow-specific effect
examples.observed: The G4-seq row shows a reference read, removal of the read fragment, renewed primer hybridization, addition of K+ or PDS to stabilize G4 regions, a second read with polymerase stalls, and comparison of reads.
examples.safe_to_encode: PDS is a reagent option at a particular operation with the source-stated stabilization effect; contrast conditions and observed readout matter as well as chemical identity.
examples.not_established: The PDS structure alone does not establish this role, nor does common PDS usage establish that two methods are descendants or interchangeable.

examples.observed: First cDNA synthesis uses a dTTP-containing nucleotide mixture; second-strand synthesis is labeled with dUTP and the corresponding strand carries U symbols. The amplification panel marks that strand with Block polymerase.
examples.safe_to_encode: Which strand acquires uracil, at which copying operation, and the depicted consequence during amplification. A generic DNA state would lose the differentiating information.
examples.not_established: Do not fill in an unshown enzyme identity or an unshown uracil-removal reaction from familiarity with other stranded RNA-seq protocols.

examples.example: TruSeq RNA Access and Nextera Library Preparation
examples.role: non-equivalent uses of broad workflow operations
examples.observed: RNA Access depicts biotinylated target probes hybridized to library targets, streptavidin magnetic-bead capture and elution. Nextera depicts adaptor-loaded transposase acting on DNA, tagmentation and amplification.
examples.safe_to_encode: Capture through a probe-associated biotin tag differs from direct molecular biotinylation; tagmentation combines fragmentation and adaptor introduction within the depicted block.
examples.not_established: Shared words such as capture or adaptor addition do not establish the same transformation, identical linkage chemistry, or historical inheritance.

conclusion: The posters mix molecular structures, schematic transformations, workflow context and navigation artwork. They should not all become operation nodes.

Record a chemical entity/feature separately from what a particular operation does to it. A useful operation comparison includes substrate features, action, resulting features, attachment relationship and readout consequence where depicted.

Several technologies share preparation or readout stages while differing in one selective chemical operation, the stage at which a tag is attached, or which strand/fraction retains the tag. This is an observed comparison strategy, not a universal fixed chain.
Chemical structure or formula can improve identification of specific reagents and reactive handles, but cannot replace molecule association, compartment, barcode attribution or operation order.

Cross-method correspondence may compare these evidenced transformations. Evolutionary edges still need the paper-specific claim of adoption/change and the older source; no historical edge is established by this review.
review_limits: Source drawings are simplified and may contain caption/label errors.
No SMILES, InChI, molecular formula or atom-mapped reaction was inferred from an image.
No new ontology/schema code, native model calls, or canonical method connections were created.
